newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS- US debt vols steady after data.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS- US debt vols steady after data.

text.p: Implied volatilities for U.S. debt futures options were steady to very slightly softer in early afternoon trade on Friday as the market turned its attention to the slew of U.S. economic data due next week.
Among the key numbers scheduled for release next week are nonfarm payrolls, the National Association of Purchasing Managers index and new home sales.

Just after noon CDT/1700 GMT, implied volatility for March eurodollar options was down 0.50 percentage point at 14.4 percent. Implied volatility for June was 0.10 percentage point lower on the day at 16.8 percent, dealers said.
However, one dealer at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange said the March level was skewed by one large trade and otherwise would also be fairly flat.
An investment house bought 10,000 March 94.25 calls and sold 15,000 March 94.50 calls, he said.
"It probably would mean the locals are leaning on that 94.25 strike a little bit, which is probably why the March is off a bit," he said.
John Nyhoff, chief economist at Mitsubishi Financial Futures Inc, said volatilities show the market does not anticipate significant price movement, despite upcoming data.
"I think the phenomenon behind volatility is that nobody truly anticipates that there's going to be any kind of major breakout next week," he said.
He said the only contract showing significant volatility movement was the "short December," an option which is priced off the 1997 December contract but expires in December 1996.
That volatility has risen 2.0 percent over the last week to 21.0/21.6 percent, he said.
However, he said that option is particularly sensitive to any change in the yield curve, and therefore to even faint nervousness in the market.
A dealer at the Chicago Board of Trade disagreed with Nyhoff's view that the market does not expect a break.
Implied volatility for December T-bond futures options was down 0.10 percentage point at 10.8/10.9 percent.
The dealer said that level was somewhat higher than might be expected, given that the contract remains rangebound and that volatilities normally fall on a Friday.
"It's sort of like it's coiling," he said of the underlying futures contract. He said T-bond options traders are becoming increasingly nervous that the market will break up or down soon.

By early afternoon, the debt futures markets had absorbed much higher-than-forecast durable goods data for September. Durable goods orders rose 4.6 percent versus estimates for an increase of 2.0 percent. Bond futures fell on the number but then strengthened as traders looked at ex-transportation orders, which rose only 0.9 percent.
The market gained further after September U.S. existing home sales came in lower than expected, falling 2.9 percent.

Nyhoff said the latter data appeared to have the greatest impact on the market. "That seems to be the major bullish catalyst of the day." -Danielle Bochove (312)408-8750,E-mail:derivatives@reuters.com
